item.title: Steves: In Europe, make your memento-shopping memorable
item.description:
With each trip I take, I look for cultural souvenirs — experiences and memories are the gold nuggets of travel. Shopping is never my priority, but when I do bring mementos home I find the best souvenirs come from local entrepreneurs and craftspeople. These days, Europe’s modern shopping arenas are also fun spots to witness a slice of contemporary life. In moderation, it can be fun to immerse yourself in the retail culture of Europe’s grandest cities.

The post Steves: In Europe, make your memento-shopping memorable appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Carrier USS Abraham Lincoln Pulls into Guam for Logistics Stop, Deployment Now at 302 Days
item.description: Carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), the embarked Carrier Air Wing 9 and the guided-missile destroyer USS Frank Petersen (DDG-121) pulled into Guam on Saturday, according to a statement from U.S. 7th Fleet. Lincoln exited the South China Sea this week via the Sulu Sea, according to ship spotters, and arrived at Apra Harbor for a logistics stop. “The stop on Naval Base Guam marks [Carrier Strike Group]-3 personnel’s first return to American soil in nine months, during which personnel will be afforded on-base liberty,” reads the statement. The post visit to Guam follows the carrier’s port visit to Pattaya, Thailand

Dubbed the Naval Affordable Interceptor, the concept seeks to field a container launcher that can carry at least 60 missiles. The system’s installation should not require permanent modification aboard its host warship. Interested firms should be able to produce 500 interceptors annually and operationally deploy the system within 12 months of award. The white paper’s request and requirements for the low-cost interceptors are for the first system planned to be procured by the Navy’s Portfolio

item.title: Governor submits formal comments on proposed federal offshore mineral lease sale
item.description:
“Learn first. Protect what sustains us. Make informed decisions.”
Source: ASG press release

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Governor Pulaali‘i Nikolao Pula has submitted his formal comments to the U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) regarding the proposed PACM-1 offshore mineral lease sale.

The Governor’s comments were informed by public comments submitted to his office, the work of the Deep-Sea Minerals Steering Committee, input from territorial agencies and subject-matter experts, and the views, concerns, and perspectives on deep-sea minerals that members of the community have shared publicly over the past year.

Governor Pulaali‘i thanks the many members of the community who took the time to submit comments, ask questions, share information, and express their concerns and perspectives. He also recognizes the members of the Steering Committee, territorial agencies, and subject-matter experts whose contributions helped inform his final comments.

“Our people care deeply about our ocean and what we leave for future generations,” he said. “I have listened carefully to the concerns being raised, particularly about our fisheries and marine environment. Those concerns matter, and they are reflected in the position I have submitted to the Federal Government.”

The Governor’s comments make clear that American Samoa does not support commercial deep-sea mineral extraction at this time. Significant questions remain about the potential effects of large-scale extraction on deep-ocean ecosystems, fisheries, and the broader marine environment.

At the same time, Governor Pulaali‘i recognizes that the proposed lease areas are in federal waters outside American Samoa’s territorial jurisdiction and that the decision whether to proceed with the lease sale rests with the United States Government. His comments therefore focus on protecting American Samoa’s interests and ensuring that the Territory remains fully engaged as the federal process moves forward.

A central message of the Governor’s submission is that the current lease process should not be confused with authorization to commercially mine the seafloor. 

If the Federal Government proceeds, Preliminary Activities should be used to gather credible science, establish environmental baselines, better understand potential impacts, and provide information needed for future decisions. Any later proposal for commercial extraction must be treated as a separate decision and undergo the environmental, scientific, regulatory, and governmental review required at that time.

The Governor’s comments also call for strong fisheries protections, environmental monitoring and transparency, protection of Rose Atoll and other marine resources, safeguards for territorial infrastructure, meaningful opportunities for American Samoa workers and businesses, workforce development, and an equitable share for American Samoa of revenues that could result from any future offshore mineral development.

For members of the community who remain concerned about the process, Governor Pulaali‘i emphasized that no decision on commercial mining is being made today. The current process provides an opportunity to learn more, strengthen protections, and ensure that American Samoa’s interests are represented before decisions about any future commercial activity are considered.

“We should not be afraid to learn more, and we should not be pressured to decide our future before we have the information needed to make that decision,” he said. “We will remain engaged, protect what sustains our people, and insist that American Samoa’s voice is heard.”

The Governor’s comments conclude with a simple principle for American Samoa’s approach:

“Learn first. Protect what sustains us. Make informed decisions.”

item.title: Marines Test USV for Littoral Explosive Ordnance Disposal Operations
item.description: The Marine Corps trialled using an Unmanned Surface Vessel as part of its Littoral Explosive Ordnance Neutralization System last month. The USV trials were carried out by Program Manager Combat Support Systems (PM CSS) of Portfolio Acquisition Executive Marine Corps (PAE MC) with a PM CSS Explosive Hazard Defeat Team at Camp Pendleton, Calif. The trials were held in response to a littoral capability gap with the solution being a commercial USV equipped with integrated autonomous driving and payloads that consist of Sonar, Forward-Looking Infrared cameras, Line of Sight Communications and Acoustic Communications (AComms), reads a PAE MC news release

item.title: Japan Air Self-Defense Force Recon Drone Crashes into Sea of Japan
item.description: One of Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s RQ-4 Global Hawk Unmanned Aircraft System crashed into the Sea of Japan on Tuesday, the service announced. The reconnaissance drone crashed in an area approximately 50 kilometers – 31 miles – north of the Tottori Prefecture, located in the western part of Honshu. The UAS, assigned to the 502nd Squadron, Air Warning Wing based at JASDF Misawa Air Base, took off at 10:20 a.m. local time on Tuesday, according to a JASDF report on the loss. There was a communication failure with the Global Hawk around 12:55 p.m. and the drone disappeared from radar
item.source:markdown: One of Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s RQ-4 Global Hawk Unmanned Aircraft System crashed into the Sea of Japan on Tuesday, the service announced. The reconnaissance drone crashed in an area approximately 50 kilometers – 31 miles – north of the Tottori Prefecture, located in the western part of Honshu. item.title: Former and current ASTCA board members pressed on questions about spending on the American250 festivities
item.description:
New revelations come to light about ASTCA COO Chuck Leota’s severance payout
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Former and current members of the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA) appeared before the Senate Government Operations Committee Monday, where lawmakers examined how ASTCA funds were used during the American250 celebrations — and confronted new revelation that ASTCA money was used to make a child support payment for former CEO and current Chief Operations Officer Chuck Leota, without board approval.

Committee Chairman Sen. Togiola T.A. Tulafono opened the hearing by noting widespread public concern over what many view as excessive spending on the American250 festivities. He emphasized that the Fono had not appropriated any specific funding for ASTCA to participate in the celebrations.

Former board chairman Avamua Dave Haleck, former vice chairman Maota Alex Sene, former second vice chair Ella Gurr, and former board secretary Andrew Berquist testified alongside current board members Omar Shalhout (acting chairman), Lewis Seau, Karen Satele, and Molitogi Lemana.

Avamua, who resigned from the board in July 2026 after the celebrations, said he stepped down to focus on his family businesses. When pressed by Togiola and Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean on whether other factors influenced his resignation, he repeatedly stated that business and family obligations were the only reasons.

Avamua and Maota explained that the American250 budget was drawn from ASTCA’s FY2026 marketing allocation, which totaled just over $1 million. They said that once the budget was approved, the ASTCA CEO had full authority to spend the funds.

The CEO presented the celebration plans to the board, and ASTCA funded the event in partnership with The Reid Group, with additional contributions from other government departments.

When asked how much of the marketing budget was earmarked for the celebrations, Avamua said the CEO informed the board that between $200,000 and $300,000 would be spent.

Senator Togiola sought confirmation that board minutes existed documenting approval for the American250 spending. Former board secretary Andrew Berquist said he no longer had access to the email drive containing the minutes because he rescinded his access after resigning.

He said the electronic records were turned over to ASTCA legal counsel William Ledoux, who currently resides off‑island, and board member Lewis Seau. Togiola requested that the committee be provided with all minutes related to the American250 discussions.

CHILD SUPPORT PAYMENT BY ASTCA

The hearing took a sharp turn when Senate President Tuaolo asked Avamua whether the board had approved $100,000 for a child support payment made on behalf of former CEO Chuck Leota to the High Court.

Avamua confirmed the payment had been made — but insisted it was not the reason he resigned.

Tuaolo pressed further: “Who approved it? Did the board approve $100,000 for Chuck’s child support?”

Former vice chair Ella Gurr responded. She explained that Leota’s severance package was under discussion, and the board had considered transitioning him into a career service position as Chief Operations Officer instead of issuing a severance payout.

She said the child support payment was raised during board discussions, but the majority of the board did not support it, and the matter was tabled.

According to Gurr, the ASTCA CEO then sought approval directly from the Governor, who approved the payment. The board only learned about it afterward.

Tuaolo asked again whether the board had approved the payment. Avamua confirmed:

“No, the board did not approve it.”

He also confirmed that the Governor had approved the payment.

Senator Togiola asked where the money came from. Avamua said the payment was issued from ASTCA’s general account, and the check was made out to the High Court of American Samoa.

Samoa News will report further in tomorrow’s issue on ASTCA CEO Folasaitu Sorepa Thomas’ answers to direct questioning that took place on Monday morning during the Fono’s joint budget hearing regarding the controversial child support payment made on behalf of former CEO Chuck Leota using ASTCA funds.

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
American250 festivities

item.title: Obituaries for September 16
item.description:
David Kalani Kaili Calles, Sr., 99, of Hilo died Aug. 1 at Hale Anuenue Restorative Care Center. Born in Hilo, he was a retired clerk for Young Brothers Ltd., U.S. Army veteran trained with several bodybuilding clubs, won the title 1950 Mr. Big Island HI, coached women’s volleyball, supported and participated in Haili volleyball tournaments, served as 1952 USA Commissioner Volleyball District Hilo was co-founder of the Hilo Ohana Horseshoe Pitchers Club, former member of HSHPA and NHPA Horseshoe Pitchers associations and, in 2009, the horseshoe courts at Onekahakaha Beach Park were dedicated to him. Visitation 9-10 a.m. Monday (Sep. 21) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Eulogy and memories until 10:45 a.m. Burial to follow at the Hawaii Veterans Cemetery #2. Casual attire. Survived by son, David (Claudia) Calles Jr. of Hilo; daughter, Darlene (Amanda) Calles-Christian of Hilo; stepdaughters, April (Ronald) Supalo of Chicago and Louise (Cornelius) Tarr of Utah; grandchildren, great grandchildren, cousins, nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 16 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Carrier USS Abraham Lincoln Operates with Australians in the South China Sea
item.description: USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) recently operated with Royal Australian Navy frigates in the South China Sea, the Australian Department of Defense announced Tuesday. Frigates HMAS Perth (FFH157) and HMAS Stuart (FFH153) supported the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group during its transit of the South China Sea in accordance with international law, according to a news release. “Australian Defense Force and the U.S. routinely train and operate together, increasing interoperability between our forces and strengthening our collective capabilities,” reads the release. The news release did not disclose when the Australian frigates supported the U.S. strike group in the South China Sea.

item.title: Amata congratulates Dr. Mata’uitafā Temukisa Solomona Fai’ai on Yale Doctorate
item.description:
Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata congratulates Dr. Mata’uitafā Temukisa Solomona Fai’ai, Ph.D., M.P.H., on earning her doctorate in Chronic Disease Epidemiology from Yale University. Her doctoral research focused on cardiometabolic health among adolescents in American Samoa.

“Congratulations to Dr. Mata’uitafā on this outstanding academic achievement and the dedication and perseverance that brought her to this milestone,” said Congresswoman Amata. “It is especially meaningful to see a daughter of American Samoa applying her education and research to improving the health of our Samoan and Pacific communities. Her accomplishments encourage our young people to pursue their educational goals and use their talents in service to others.”

Dr. Mata’uitafā is from Leone, Tutuila; Olosega, Manu’a; and Safune, Savai’i. She earned her Ph.D. in Chronic Disease Epidemiology through the Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, completing her doctoral training in the Yale School of Public Health.

She is continuing her work in Pacific public health as a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Global Health Emerging Scholars (GHES) Fellowship Program through Yale University, in collaboration with the Samoa Ministry of Health Collaborative Research Center. Her fellowship focuses on using social network analysis to understand peer influences on adolescent health and inform culturally relevant interventions addressing noncommunicable disease risk among Samoan adolescents.

“Earning a doctorate from Yale is a testament to what is possible for a girl born and raised in American Samoa: to pursue her dreams and receive a world-class education while remaining deeply rooted in her family and community,” said Dr. Mata’uitafā. “I hope my journey reflects the strength and resilience of Pasefika women, who often pursue our aspirations while caring for and uplifting our families.”

“American Samoa is proud of Dr. Mata’uitafā and all that she has accomplished,” continued Congresswoman Amata. “Her example demonstrates the importance of education, determination, and using our abilities in service to others. Fa’amalo and congratulations to Dr. Mata’uitafā and her family.”

item.title: Vaitogi ‘SA’ commences at 6 p.m.
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Vaitogi village will be observing and enforcing their annual curfew or "SA" for this year starting at 6:00 pm today, Tuesday, September 15, 2026, and ending at 6:00 pm on Wednesday, September 16, 2026. 

The tradition dates back over a century to 1896. 

According to historical village accounts, a massive Great Fire broke out and raged violently through Vaitogi lands for days. The fire could not be controlled, destroying scores of acres of crops, vegetation, and fales, directly threatening the lives of everyone in the village. With no physical way left to combat the flames, the village chiefs gathered all the residents together to pray for divine intervention.

Local tradition states that immediately following their unified prayers, a miraculous heavy rain fell and completely extinguished the fire. 

To honor this miracle, the village council established the first official 24-hour sā in 1897. It has been strictly observed every year since, traditionally taking place from 6:00 PM on September 15th to 6:00 PM on September 16th.

item.title: Western Pacific scientists chart research needs for reopened fisheries
item.description:
Source: Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council

HONOLULU  — The Scientific and Statistical Committee (SSC) of the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council concluded its three-day meeting Thursday. 

For the American Samoa longline fishery, the SSC said if the Council decides to change existing turtle-related gear requirements, the Council should ask the Pacific  Islands Fisheries Science Center (PIFSC) to use observer data to evaluate potential effects on turtle interactions and on target and nontarget catch, particularly silky and oceanic whitetip sharks. 

Members highlighted that environmental changes and other basin-wide factors can also influence turtle interaction rates, complicating comparisons of fishery performance before and after gear regulations were implemented.

Reexamining Fishing Access Around Rose Atoll

The Committee also reviewed possible changes to the Large Vessel Prohibited Area (LVPA) around Muliāva (Rose Atoll), which restricts large-vessel fishing between 12 and 50 nautical miles from the atoll.

Members noted the LVPA did not prevent the decline of American Samoa’s smaller longline fleet. 

The SSC said U.S. purse seiners are unlikely to fish around Rose Atoll because of the area’s small size, although purse-seine fishing there, if it occurred, could potentially affect species targeted by the small-boat fleet. Members pointed out that large longline vessels primarily target albacore and are unlikely to compete substantially with the target species of the small-boat fleet. 

The SSC also said the South Pacific albacore stock remains healthy even as vessel numbers, participation and catch rates in the American Samoa fleet have declined.

Electronic monitoring being implemented in the longline fleet in 2027 is expected to provide additional information for evaluating fishing activity.

Looking Beyond Pounds and Dollars

Other science presented during the meeting highlighted why the effects of fishery management cannot always be measured through commercial landings alone.

PIFSC’s American Samoa Fish Flow Project found seafood from small-boat, longline and purse-seine fisheries contributes an estimated 560,000 to 859,000 meals to the local community. Small-boat catch flows extensively through families, friends, community leaders and events, with sharing often taking priority over sales. Researchers said some roadside sales, gifted fish and other forms of distribution are incompletely captured by conventional fishery statistics. 

“The value of a gifted fish likely exceeds its commercial value,” SSC member Alister Hunt said, questioning how well commercial and recreational fishery statistics capture seafood sharing and its cultural value. 

The findings complement work by the SSC’s Social Valuation Working Group, which developed four domains for considering the broader value of fisheries: food security and sovereignty, cultural importance, social cohesion, and well-being and livelihood integration. The Committee endorsed the domains for Council review.

Setting Future Research Priorities

The SSC also completed its ranking of 15 regional fishery research priorities developed with input from the Council’s Advisory Panels and Fishing Industry Advisory Committee. The priorities focus largely on evaluating fishery closures, economic and market dynamics, improving data collection and addressing depredation. The SSC recommended the Council review and adopt the final rankings. 

The Committee also recommended 2027–2030 acceptable biological catches totaling 51,510 pounds for nine American Samoa bottomfish species and endorsed the terms of reference and reviewers for the upcoming independent review of the main Hawaiian Islands deep-seven bottomfish stock assessment.

The SSC provides advice to the Council, which will meet virtually Sept. 15-17, 2026, with host sites in Hawai‘i, American Samoa, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. 

The Committee called for a deliberate, science-based approach as commercial fishing resumes in the NWHI. The SSC recommended forming a working group with Council and NOAA Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center (PIFSC) staff to develop a bottomfish data collection plan. It also recommended the Council consider an experimental fishing permit (EFP) as the fishery reopens and said any longer-term permitting regime should have a clearly defined objective.

The NWHI bottomfish fishery had been closed to commercial fishing since 2010. Before closure, the area accounted for about half of Hawai‘i bottomfish management unit species landings and supplied local markets with species specifically caught there. As fishing resumes, SSC members emphasized the need to design data collection carefully to support future spatially explicit assessments. 

“An EFP may not be the quickest way to fish, but it may be the right tool to collect data at the start,” said SSC member Shelton Harley. He added that the long period with little fishing creates an opportunity to learn more about natural mortality and growth rates. 

Scientists Support Removing Outdated Swordfish Restriction

As part of its review of actions identified under the federal Executive Order on “Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness,” the SSC agreed there is no scientific basis to retain the swordfish retention limit in the Hawai‘i deep-set longline fishery. Members noted that other sea turtle mitigation measures have been implemented, circle hooks are mandatory in the fishery and the fishery will have full electronic monitoring implementation. 

The current rule limits an unobserved deep-set vessel north of the equator to 25 swordfish per trip when using circle hooks and 10 with other hooks. The restriction originated when the Hawai‘i shallow-set swordfish fishery was closed under a court order more than two decades ago, with the intent of preventing vessels engaging in deep-set fishing from transitioning to shallow-set fishing while at sea. Since the limit was last modified in 2012, deep-set vessels have averaged fewer than five swordfish per trip. 

For two other Seafood Executive Order priorities, the SSC identified analyses needed to inform the Council’s management decisions. 

For the Hawai‘i shallow-set fishery, PIFSC reported that it is developing a model to estimate loggerhead and leatherback turtle interactions with and without trip limits, with the results to inform updated population assessments. The Committee asked Council and PIFSC staff to coordinate with its protected species working group before the December meeting for updates and continued discussion of the technical analyses that will inform Council decision-making.

Online: Via Webex: https://tinyurl.com/208CouncilMtg

Event password: CM208mtg

item.title: Houthis Make Moves On Red Sea, U.S., Iran Go Tanker for Warship
item.description: The Houthis in Yemen have seized Perim Island, a parcel of land that lies in the Red Sea in an amphibious assault, giving the Iranian-backed group a strategic foothold over the Bab el-Mandeb. The Houthis’ push this week – first taking Mocha on the Red Sea’s North Coast, then Perim Island – coincides with escalating tensions between Iran and the U.S., with Washington establishing that for any warship to come under attack, it will strike an Iranian tanker. It is not immediately clear what the Houthis’ movement will mean for the ongoing U.S.-Iran war. The Yemini group shut down shipping

item.title: Remembering September 11 after 25 years
item.description:
compiled by Samoa News staff

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Twenty-five years ago today, in just a little over two hours on Tuesday, September 11, 2001, 2,977 innocent souls perished in the most despicable act of terror in the history of our country. Yet amid the wreckage and carnage of that day, the world witnessed the courage, valor, and patriotism of America.

Earlier this week the White House issued the following Presidential Proclamation: 

A quarter of a century has passed since the terrible day of September 11, 2001, and an entire generation of Americans has now come of age with no living memory of that fateful day.  The passage of time must never dim what will forever burn bright in the conscience of our Nation.  Amid the ashes of Ground Zero, we made a solemn vow to Never Forget — a vow that must be renewed in every American heart, taught in every classroom, and honored in every community across our land.  

Twenty-five years ago, beneath a clear September sky, the peace of our Nation was shattered when radical Islamic terrorists hijacked four commercial jet planes and converted them into weapons of mass murder.  

At 8:46 a.m. American Airlines Flight 11 was deliberately flown into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York City.  Shadowing closely behind was United Airlines Flight 175 and within a span of 17 minutes, the South Tower was struck.  At that moment, it became clear that our Nation was under attack.  Before the morning had passed, both soaring towers — the premier symbols of American economic strength and prosperity — had collapsed into the city below, claiming thousands of innocent lives and leaving behind unfathomable destruction.  The time was 10:28 a.m.

Just 34 minutes later, at the edge of our Nation’s capital in Arlingtion, Virginia, American Airlines Flight 77 was flown into the Pentagon, the fortress of American military might, striking down members of our Armed Forces and dedicated civil servants.  Amid smoke and flames, survivors turned back into the burning building to carry survivors to safety.  

But the horror of that morning was not over. Aboard United Airlines Flight 93, passengers learned through frantic cellphone calls of the terror already unfolding in New York and Virginia. Knowing that their plane was being used as a weapon, they resolved to fight back.  Among them was Todd Beamer, a devoted husband, father, and man of deep faith, who calmly led his fellow passengers in a recitation of the Lord’s Prayer before speaking his last, immortal words:  “Are you ready? Okay. Let’s roll.”  With those immortal words, the heroes of Flight 93 mounted a daring assault on the hijackers and forced the aircraft down in a field outside of Shanksville, Pennslvania, just 20 minutes flying time from their intended target of our Nation’s capital. In laying down their lives, those 40 patriots transformed a quiet field into hallowed ground — leaving behind an everlasting testament to the unbreakable will of the American people. 

In just a little over two hours on Tuesday, September 11, 2001, 2,977 innocent souls perished in the most despicable act of terror in the history of our country. Yet amid the wreckage and carnage of that day, the world witnessed the courage, valor, and patriotism of America. Members of the New York City Police Department, the Fire Department of the City of New York, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, worked around the clock beside almost 100 emergency and first responder agencies to save those still trapped in the rubble and ensure the safe evacuation of untold thousands of New York City residents. Rescue workers, medical personnel, and thousands of volunteers answered the call, risking their own lives and giving everything they had to help fellow Americans.  

In the hours and days that followed September 11, 2001, our Nation came together with a unity and purpose that is distinctively American. We mourned as one people. We prayed as one Nation. We resolved, with iron will, that those who attacked us would feel the full measure of American strength. The terrorists sought to break our spirit — they failed. They sought to divide us — they could not. They sought to make us afraid — instead, they awakened the mightiest force for justice the world has ever known.

In the days, months, and years that followed, thousands of American patriots stepped forward to wear the uniform of the United States Armed Forces. They left behind their families and communities, crossed oceans, and carried the fight to our enemies in distant battlefields so the horrors of that September morning would never again reach our shores. For nearly a quarter century, an entire generation of warriors served, fought, and sacrificed in defense of our freedom. Many gave their last full measure of devotion, and countless others returned home bearing the seen and unseen wounds of war. Our Nation owes them a debt that can never be repaid. 

That September morning changed our country forever, teaching us that oceans alone could no longer shield our homeland from the forces of evil, that liberty must always be guarded by a free and vigilant people, and that the strength of our Republic will always prevail. As President, I have no higher duty than to ensure the safety and well-being of the American People, and from the very first day I returned to office, my Administration has been unwavering in its commitment to ensure that our Nation is defended by the strongest and most lethal military the world has ever known. I will never hesitate to protect our country by enforcing a foreign policy of peace through strength, bringing swift justice to our enemies wherever they hide, and vigorously defending our national security interests at home and abroad.

Today, the hatred that struck us on September 11 still exists, and the lessons of that day remain as urgent as ever.  We must defend our sovereignty, our values, and our sacred birthright to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.  We must protect our treasured way of life against all those who seek our destruction — whether they threaten us from foreign lands or from among us within our borders.  Most of all, we must ensure that the memory of September 11 never fades into history, but remains a living inheritance passed from one generation of Americans to the next.

For millions of Americans, the memories of September 11, 2001, remain as vivid today as they were 25 years ago. We will never forget the 2,977 precious lives taken from us, we will always cherish their memories, and we will forever hold their families in the enduring embrace of ourNation. We stand in unending gratitude to the first responders who answered the call of duty, including the thousands who continue to suffer from serious health conditions caused by their service.  We honor the warriors of our Armed Forces who have defended the sacred cause of freedom in the quarter century since. Above all, we ask Almighty God to keep our Republic forever safe, forever united, and forever free.

By a joint resolution approved December 18, 2001 (Public Law 107-89), the Congress designated September 11 of each year as “Patriot Day” and likewise, this year President Donald J. Trump has proclaimed September 11, 2026, as Patriot Day, 2026:

 I call upon all departments, agencies, and instrumentalities of the United States to display the Flag of the United States at half-staff in honor of the 2,977 victims of the attacks of September 11, 2001. I also invite the Governors of the United States and its Territories, and interested organizations and individuals, to join in this observance.  

Signed: Donald J. Trump

Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata is commemorating the 25th anniversary of September 11, 2001, in memory of the lost lives and heroic stories that are now part of our national history:

“Twenty-five years have passed since the terrible attacks of September 11th that changed much about our country and the world,” said Aumua Amata. “My own view was the sight of dark smoke rising high into the sky from the Pentagon, first from where I was that morning at the Capitol, then for hours from my car as I tried to get through the chaos of traffic, driving close by the Pentagon, and finally still seeing endless smoke many hours later. 

“On this 25th anniversary, we remember that thousands of families feel the deeply personal loss of loved ones. We honor the great numbers of firefighters, police and responders who rescued others, and headed up the towers and toward the danger, many at the sacrifice of their own precious lives. We think of the bravery of those aboard Flight 93, where there’s now a somber Memorial site in Pennsylvania. The site of the World Trade Center towers is now a powerful National Museum in New York while across the street the One World Trade Center stands gleaming in the sun, built even higher in a testament to the American spirit. 

“Today, a special thank you to all our law enforcement, firefighters, and first responders – current and retired – for your service. We depend on you in times of crisis, and support the ongoing priority of the best possible equipment and training. Thank you also to our many Toa o Samoa, and all our U.S. Service Members and Veterans nationwide. 

“We also remember that 25 years ago we experienced a strong and special unity of spirit, a turn toward faith, and patriotic responsibility. For a time, partisanship, bickering and gridlock ceased. May we continue to find togetherness as a country and courage to uphold the cause of freedom. Most of all, may we be again reminded to look to God for hope and wisdom. May God bless American Samoa and the United States.”

AS DEMS honor the Fallen in Remembrance of 9/11 and issued the following statement:

Today, we pause in solemn remembrance of the thousands of innocent lives lost on September 11, 2001. We honor the victims, the brave first responders, service members, and all those whose courage and sacrifice inspired a nation during one of the darkest days in American history. 

We call on our communities to remember the fallen, honor the heroes, and reflect on the strength, resilience, and unity that carried our nation forward. Their memory reminds us that our shared values are stronger than hate and fear. 

The lessons of September 11 continue to guide our responsibility to safeguard future generations while upholding the freedom and principles that define our nation, reminding us that security and liberty must always go hand in hand. 

May we never forget those we lost, those who answered the call to serve, and the enduring spirit of a nation united in remembrance.

I will never hesitate to protect our country by enforcing a foreign policy of peace through strength, bringing swift justice to our enemies wherever they hide, and vigorously defending our national security interests at home and abroad.
Today, the hatred that struck us on September 11 still exists, and the lessons of that day remain as urgent as ever. We must defend our sovereignty, our values, and our sacred birthright to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. We must protect our treasured way of life against all those who seek our destruction — whether they threaten us from foreign lands or from among us within our borders. Most of all, we must ensure that the memory of September 11 never fades into history, but remains a living inheritance passed from one generation of Americans to the next.
For millions of Americans, the memories of September 11, 2001, remain as vivid today as they were 25 years ago. We will never forget the 2,977 precious lives taken from us, we will always cherish their memories, and we will forever hold their families in the enduring embrace of ourNation. We stand in unending gratitude to the first responders who answered the call of duty, including the thousands who continue to suffer from serious health conditions caused by their service. We honor the warriors of our Armed Forces who have defended the sacred cause of freedom in the quarter century since. Above all, we ask Almighty God to keep our Republic forever safe, forever united, and forever free.
By a joint resolution approved December 18, 2001 (Public Law 107-89), the Congress designated September 11 of each year as “Patriot Day” and likewise, this year President Donald J. Trump has proclaimed September 11, 2026, as Patriot Day, 2026:
I call upon all departments, agencies, and instrumentalities of the United States to display the Flag of the United States at half-staff in honor of the 2,977 victims of the attacks of September 11, 2001. I also invite the Governors of the United States and its Territories, and interested organizations and individuals, to join in this observance.
_Signed: Donald J. Trump_
Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata is commemorating the 25th anniversary of September 11, 2001, in memory of the lost lives and heroic stories that are now part of our national history:
“Twenty-five years have passed since the terrible attacks of September 11th that changed much about our country and the world,” said Aumua Amata. “My own view was the sight of dark smoke rising high into the sky from the Pentagon, first from where I was that morning at the Capitol, then for hours from my car as I tried to get through the chaos of traffic, driving close by the Pentagon, and finally still seeing endless smoke many hours later.
“On this 25th anniversary, we remember that thousands of families feel the deeply personal loss of loved ones. We honor the great numbers of firefighters, police and responders who rescued others, and headed up the towers and toward the danger, many at the sacrifice of their own precious lives. We think of the bravery of those aboard Flight 93, where there’s now a somber Memorial site in Pennsylvania. The site of the World Trade Center towers is now a powerful National Museum in New York while across the street the One World Trade Center stands gleaming in the sun, built even higher in a testament to the American spirit.
“Today, a special thank you to all our law enforcement, firefighters, and first responders – current and retired – for your service. We depend on you in times of crisis, and support the ongoing priority of the best possible equipment and training. Thank you also to our many Toa o Samoa, and all our U.S. Service Members and Veterans nationwide.
“We also remember that 25 years ago we experienced a strong and special unity of spirit, a turn toward faith, and patriotic responsibility. For a time, partisanship, bickering and gridlock ceased. May we continue to find togetherness as a country and courage to uphold the cause of freedom. Most of all, may we be again reminded to look to God for hope and wisdom. May God bless American Samoa and the United States.”
AS DEMS honor the Fallen in Remembrance of 9/11 and issued the following statement:
Today, we pause in solemn remembrance of the thousands of innocent lives lost on September 11, 2001. We honor the victims, the brave first responders, service members, and all those whose courage and sacrifice inspired a nation during one of the darkest days in American history.
We call on our communities to remember the fallen, honor the heroes, and reflect on the strength, resilience, and unity that carried our nation forward. Their memory reminds us that our shared values are stronger than hate and fear.
The lessons of September 11 continue to guide our responsibility to safeguard future generations while upholding the freedom and principles that define our nation, reminding us that security and liberty must always go hand in hand.
May we never forget those we lost, those who answered the call to serve, and the enduring spirit of a nation united in remembrance.

item.title: A Legacy of Learning: American Samoa DOE and UH Mānoa close chapter on 45-Year Teacher Preparation Partnership
item.description:
By 
Lori Fulton and Jon Yoshioka

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Fa'afetai lava and Mahalo Nui Loa! For forty-five years, the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (UH Mānoa) College of Education's School of Teacher Education (STE) has had the honor of partnering with the American Samoa Department of Education (ASDOE) to support and certify educators across American Samoa. 

As the ASDOE moves forward to explore new pathways for teacher certification, this cherished partnership will formally conclude in December 2026. We wish them every success in that endeavor.

The program's roots stretch back to 1981, when it was established as the Territorial Teacher Training Assistance Project (TTTAP). Over time, it grew and evolved into the UH Mānoa American Samoa Bachelor of Education (BEd) program. 

Its mission remained constant throughout: to provide in-service teachers in American Samoa with the content knowledge and pedagogical skills to strengthen instruction in their own classrooms. Funded through ASDOE via federal sources, the program made teacher certification accessible to educators who were already serving their communities.

That mission translated into something remarkable. 

Over the course of four decades, nearly 900 teachers earned certification in Elementary Education, Elementary and Special Education, or Elementary and Early Childhood Education. Many went on to complete their Master's degrees and continue to serve the people of American Samoa in meaningful ways. The reach of this program lives on in every classroom those educators have touched.

A partnership of this length and impact is built by many hands, and we are grateful to everyone who contributed over the years. Though they would be the last to seek recognition, we feel compelled to honor a group of individuals whose dedication went far beyond what was asked of them — people who created lasting, life-changing experiences for their students.

We recognize Dr. Laura Falealii-Laolagi, the program's current Director, whose leadership has been a steady and guiding force. Ronald Turituri and Sarah Chan Kau-Tuiolemotu have served with distinction as current faculty, bringing expertise and care to every student they teach. William Thompson and Mene Tauaa, who faithfully served as faculty for many years and continue to teach courses, have embodied the spirit of this program from its earliest days.

Working alongside Laura, Ron, Sarah, Will, and Mene gave UH Mānoa and Hawaiʻi educators some of the most rewarding professional experiences of their lives. Everyone was welcomed as family.

The opportunity to learn as much as we taught — from our colleagues, our students, and the community of American Samoa — is something those of us in the STE will carry with us always.

A hui hou — until we meet again.

Local News
Tags: 
UH School of Teacher Education (STE)

item.title: Obituaries for September 10
item.description:
Conrad Byron Alicuben, 89, of Hilo died Aug. 8 at Yukio Okutsu State Veterans Home. Born in Hilo, he was a retired electrical inspector supervisor for the county, the former Sheraton Waiakea Village and the former Hilo Coast Processing Co., and U.S. Air Force veteran. Visitation 4-5 p.m. Monday (Sep. 14) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Memorial service at 5 p.m. Private family committal service with military honors Tuesday (Sep. 15) at East Hawaii Veterans Cemetery No. 2 Pavilion. Survived by wife, Peggy Alicuben of Hilo; son, Conrad “Cy” Alicuben of Hilo; daughter, Cristy (Ethan) Castillo of Hilo; hanai son, Nikolas (Nicole) Geraci of Hilo; brother, Donald (Mae) Alicuben of Hilo; sisters-in-law, Jean Haraga of Kaneohe, Oahu, and Janet Ichinose of Hilo; brothers-in-law, Gary (Alice) Ichinose of Hilo and Roy (Sandi) Ichinose of Pearl City, Oahu; five grandchildren and two great-grandchildren; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 10 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Dept. of Education kicks off 2026 sports program
item.description:
Source: ASG media release

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Last Friday morning joy and enthusiasm filled the American Samoa Department of Education main office in Utulei as leaders, educators, and families gathered to celebrate the official opening of the 2026 academic sports year. Acting Governor Pulumataala Ae Ae Jr. joined the government leaders, Department of Education leadership, high school administrators, coaches, community partners, parents, and student athletes. 

Principal Leo'o Dr. Patrick Danielson served as master of ceremonies, welcoming all guests and introducing Stake President Lotoa Lotoa Jr., who offered opening words of encouragement and led the invocation to set a positive tone for the event. In his special remarks, Acting Governor Pulumataala expressed immense gratitude for the continuation of student sports programs. Recalling a visit to Afono Elementary School's new gymnasium, where he noticed a lack of sports equipment and later returned to donate essential items, he reaffirmed his dedication to finding resources and funding for ASDOE athletics. He urged student athletes to strive for excellence in both academics and sports, while encouraging them to make healthy choices that support a long and fulfilling life. 

ASDOE Director Maefau Dr. Mary Taufete'e expressed her sincere appreciation to all community partners, departments, and sports associations that joined forces with the department. Emphasizing the power of collaboration, she noted that building a strong network of support, much like a house supported by many posts, ensures a brighter future for the territory's youth. The program reached an exciting highlight with the ceremonial first throw. Acting Governor Pulumataala threw the first football to a student athlete of Tafuna High School, followed by Director Taufete'e alongside House representatives and community partners, threw sports balls to student team captains from all of the high schools to officially kick off the season. 

Principal Leo'o Dr. Patrick Danielson delivered closing remarks on behalf of the Director and the Department of Education, expressing gratitude to the attendees for their presence in celebrating this significant occasion. Representative Faimealelei Allen took to the podium to offer remarks of appreciation, wishing ASDOE and its student athletes a successful year while pledging ongoing support from the legislature. The memorable gathering concluded with a closing prayer led by Stake President Lotoa Lotoa Jr.

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
2026 academic sports year

ASDOE Director Maefau Dr. Mary Taufete'e expressed her sincere appreciation to all community partners, departments, and sports associations that joined forces with the department. Emphasizing the power of collaboration, she noted that building a strong network of support, much like a house supported by many posts, ensures a brighter future for the territory's youth. The program reached an exciting highlight with the ceremonial first throw. Acting Governor Pulumataala threw the first football to a student athlete of Tafuna High School, followed by Director Taufete'e alongside House representatives and community partners, threw sports balls to student team captains from all of the high schools to officially kick off the season.
Principal Leo'o Dr. Patrick Danielson delivered closing remarks on behalf of the Director and the Department of Education, expressing gratitude to the attendees for their presence in celebrating this significant occasion. Representative Faimealelei Allen took to the podium to offer remarks of appreciation, wishing ASDOE and its student athletes a successful year while pledging ongoing support from the legislature. The memorable gathering concluded with a closing prayer led by Stake President Lotoa Lotoa Jr.

item.title: Obituaries for September 9
item.description:
Conrad Byron Alicuben, 89, of Hilo died Aug. 8 at Yukio Okutsu State Veterans Home. Born in Hilo, he was a retired electrical inspector supervisor for the county, the former Sheraton Waiakea Village and the former Hilo Coast Processing Co., and U.S. Air Force veteran. Visitation 4-5 p.m. Monday (Sep. 14) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Memorial service at 5 p.m. Private family committal service with military honors Tuesday (Sep. 15) at East Hawaii Veterans Cemetery No. 2 Pavilion. Survived by son, Conrad “Cy” Alicuben of Hilo; daughter, Cristy (Ethan) Castillo of Hilo; hanai son, Nikolas (Nicole) Geraci of Hilo; brother, Donald (Mae) Alicuben of Hilo; sisters-in-law, Jean Haraga of Kaneohe, Oahu, and Janet Ichinose of Hilo; brothers-in-law, Gary (Alice) Ichinose of Hilo and Roy (Sandi) Ichinose of Pearl City, Oahu; five grandchildren and two great-grandchildren; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

item.title: Alaska Court of Appeals dismisses voter misconduct indictment against Am Samoan woman
item.description:
By 
Right to Democracy staff

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Alaska Court of Appeals, in a unanimous opinion, has ruled against the State of Alaska in its criminal prosecution of Tupe Smith, an American Samoan woman living in Whittier who had been instructed by local officials to mark she was a “U.S. citizen” on voter registration forms after she told them she was a “U.S. national.” 

The Court ruled that to prove voter misconduct the state must establish “that the defendant acted with a consciousness of wrongdoing in purposely or deliberately making a false sworn statement under an oath.” The decision reversed an earlier ruling by the Alaska Superior Court.

“The state’s prosecution against me and my family has been extremely difficult. I feel vindicated by today’s court decision. But at the same time I worry it will not mean the end of the state’s criminal targeting of the American Samoan community in Whittier,” said Tupe Smith, who the State arrested on charges of voter misconduct shortly after she was elected to serve on her local school board in 2023. 

The Court ruled that “Smith would not be criminally liable if she did not realize that checking the U.S. citizen box was wrong,” explaining that “she stated that she had been told by Whittier election officials that if there was not a box to check for U.S. national, she should check the box for U.S. citizen.” The Court further noted that when the police interviewed her “she was confused about her status and her eligibility to vote,” with the court observing that “Alaska law sometimes expressly treats U.S. nationals as U.S. citizens.” 

“We appreciate the Court’s thoughtful ruling, which in addition to following the law just makes common sense,” said Neil Weare, Co-Director of Right to Democracy, who represents Ms. Smith along with her husband Michael Pese, who is also facing prosecution. “Being confused about what box to check, especially after public officials tell you to check a certain box, should not be considered a crime at all, much less a felony that could mean up to five years in jail.”

“We are delighted for Ms. Smith, whose case has always centered on a simple principle: people should not face felony charges for voter misconduct absent proof that they intended to do something wrong. The Alaska Court of Appeals’ opinion faithfully applies the law and provides important guidance on how Alaska’s voter-misconduct statute should be understood in future cases,” said Whitney Brown, a partner at Stoel Rives, who argued the case before the Alaska Court of Appeals on behalf of Ms. Smith.

“The state should take this moment to pause and reconsider its criminal prosecution of American Samoans in Whittier. Not just of Ms. Smith, but her husband Michael Pese and all the others it has charged,” said Charles Ala’ilima, an American Samoan attorney who also represents Ms. Smith and Mr. Pese. “American Samoa’s Governor, Congresswoman, and legislative leaders have all expressed concerns about Alaska’s ongoing criminal prosecutions of our people, and we hope Alaska prosecutors will take that into consideration as they plan their next steps.” 

If the state chooses not to bring its criminal prosecution to an end, it has a few options. The State could appeal the decision to the Alaska Supreme Court. Or it could re-indict Ms. Smith under the correct standard for voter misconduct. While it is also possible the State could charge Ms. Smith with perjury charges as it has her husband, Michael Pese, and other American Samoan defendants, the Court of Appeals questioned in a footnote whether the State could do so. Without deciding the question, it observed that “the State could potentially charge Smith with both first-degree voter misconduct and perjury, notwithstanding the fact that the legislature has chosen to enact a specialized voter misconduct statute.”

In the remaining criminal cases, the Alaska superior court is also considering motions to dismiss the charges based on the constitutional defense that Mr. Pese and others born in American Samoa - a U.S. territory for 125 years – are U.S. citizens based on the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Briefing on those motions will be complete later this month.

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ The Alaska Court of Appeals, in a unanimous opinion, has ruled against the State of Alaska in its criminal prosecution of Tupe Smith, an American Samoan woman living in Whittier who had been instructed by local officials to mark she was a “U.S. citizen” on voter registration forms after she told them she was a “U.S. national.”

The Court ruled that “Smith would not be criminally liable if she did not realize that checking the U.S. citizen box was wrong,” explaining that “she stated that she had been told by Whittier election officials that if there was not a box to check for U.S. national, she should check the box for U.S. citizen.” The Court further noted that when the police interviewed her “she was confused about her status and her eligibility to vote,” with the court observing that “Alaska law sometimes expressly treats U.S. nationals as U.S. citizens.”

item.title: Local ‘Morning Man’ featured in TV ad for the Pro Football Hall of Fame
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — NFL Network viewers in American Samoa may recognize 93KHJ Morning Man John Raynar’s voice that is featured in a TV Commercial for the Pro Football Hall of Fame. 

In the nationally televised campaign, Raynar is heard as the narrator throughout which also features 2 Time Super Bowl MVP and Steeler Hall Of Famer Lynn Swann.  

John is the long time morning show host at South Seas Broadcasting, who also runs a VoiceOver business with his wife Alice that focuses on targeting off island clients, some of which include the National Hockey League, The History Channel, Brad Pitt and character work for various video games.  

On being featured this season on the NFL Network, John Said: “It is a great honor to work on a platform that’s shared by other sons of American Samoa, Vi’i Le Atua”

item.title: Roasted Shrimp with Okra and Tomatoes
item.description:
In the South, okra and tomatoes are the crown jewels of the summer. Frying is the most common preparation for okra, but roasting also brings the best out of these two favorites; tomatoes become sweeter, and okra softens, developing a deeper savoriness brought forward by a simple seasoning of salt and pepper. Shrimp brings the dish to a new level: The smoked paprika and oregano are a perfect foil to the shrimp’s own natural, delicate flavor, and, swirled together with the olive oil and tomato juice in the pan, the result is a meal with the makings of a stew with a fraction of the time and effort. It truly tastes like a warm, summer Sunday evening. When choosing okra, go for the smaller to medium-size pods. The bigger the okra, the more likely it is to be stringy and tough. Serve with cooked rice or atop angel hair pasta.

The post Roasted Shrimp with Okra and Tomatoes appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Obituaries for September 6
item.description:
Nelson Levi Ahia, 79, of Hilo, died Aug. 11 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in Olaa, he was a retired relay technician for Hawaii Electric Light Co., U.S. Army Vietnam War veteran and member of Church of the Holy Apostles. Visitation 9-10 a.m. Monday, Sep. 14, at Church of the Holy Apostles Episcopal Church, 1407 Kapiolani St. in Hilo. Funeral Mass at 10 a.m. Burial to follow at Hawaii Veterans Cemetery No. 2. Aloha attire; no flowers. Survived by wife, Cindy Ahia; son, Dr. Chad Ahia; daughter, Jackie (Casey Morris) Ahia; siblings, James “Kimo” (Kathleen) Ahia Jr., Carol (Albert) Fajardo and Albert “Kalae” (Judy) Ahia; two grandchildren; nieces, nephews and cousins. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 6 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Obituaries for September 4
item.description:
Ralph Kuheana, 70, of Hilo died Aug. 24 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in Pahala, he was a retired housekeeper for the former Hilo Medical Center, owner of RMK Lawn Care, United Public Workers Retiree Chapter-Hawaii Sub-Chapter vice president and member of St. Joseph Catholic Church. Visitation 2-3 p.m. Tuesday, Sep. 15, at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Celebration of life at 3 p.m. Casual attire; no flowers. Survived by wife, Melba Kuheana; children, Jamelle (Benson) Galicinao, Jiselle (Benjamin) Arbeeny and Bernard (Stetson) Kuheana; siblings, Joseph Kuheana Jr., Paul Kuheana and David Kuheana; hanai sister, Mary Jane Taylor; three grandchildren; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 4 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Board of Higher Education names next ASCC President
item.description:
By 
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The American Samoa Community College Board of Higher Education has chosen a new ASCC president, replacing Interim President Sonny J. Leomiti, who had taken the position vacated by former President Dr. Rosevonne Makaiwi-Pato when her contract was not renewed by the Board this year.

In a memorandum, dated September 2, 2026, the BHE Chairperson Dr. Oreta Mapu Crichton announced to ASCC Faculty, Staff, and Students that the new ASCC President is Ti’alemasunu Tupuola Dr. Mikaele Etuale, effective Sept. 8, 2026.

Dr. Crichton expressed a special note of thanks to Interim President Leomiti for his leadership during the past months, as well as to the faculty, staff, and students for their patience, resilience, and dedication through “this period of institutional transition”.

She noted that the newly chosen ASCC president brings an outstanding track record in education and public leadership across American Samoa; and, shared the following message from the incoming president to the ASCC community:

“Saili le Atamai — To Seek Knowledge. I am incredibly honored to return to the American Samoa Community College as its President. I look forward to collaborating closely with the Board, our talented faculty, dedicated staff, and inspiring students to build upon our legacy of academic excellence and service to our territory.”

The BHE chairperson concluded her announcement with a request to “please join us in giving a warm welcome to Ti’alemasunu Tupuola Dr. Mikaele Etuale and his family as we begin this exciting next chapter together.”

BACKGROUND

It was in April this year that the BHE formally notified then ASCC president Dr. Makaiwi-Pato, who had served as the President of ASCC for nearly 26 years, in a formal letter, signed by all eight members of the Board, that, “after careful consideration, the Board has determined that it will deny your contract renewal request.”  

The letter acknowledged her extensive contributions over her long tenure, noting, “We recognize and sincerely appreciate your 25 years and 9 months of leadership and service to the college.” 

However, it also highlighted that, following recent changes in Board membership, the Board is working to establish a clear strategic direction and shared priorities for the institution's future. 

Dr. Makaiwi-Pato addressed ASCC faculty and staff in a heartfelt thank-you and farewell email sent out on the following Monday. 

In her message, she expressed sincere gratitude for their efforts in organizing a well-planned and executed graduation ceremony the previous Friday, highlighting their vital role in preparing graduates for both further education and successful entry into the workforce. 

In her email, she also conveyed her appreciation for their unwavering support and belief in her leadership throughout her time as ASCC president.

Dr. Makaiwi-Pato also shared an important update regarding her contract status, indicating she received a notice of non-renewal effective May 18, and attached the Board's letter for transparency. 

“In all professional transparency, I share this with you as the Board works toward recruitment of a new President. This comes with mixed emotions – a sadness at leaving an institution where we have worked toward our mission as a family of educators, friends, and colleagues, and at this chapter now coming to an end in my leadership. Yet I leave with a joy that I have been blessed so abundantly to have worked with professionals and dedicated, committed, and talented individuals who have left their mark in my heart.” 

In closing, Dr. Makaiwi-Pato urged her colleagues to support the BHE in its upcoming search for a new President who will lead ASCC to even greater heights. She also encouraged faculty and staff to consider taking on leadership roles themselves, emphasizing the importance of continuity and a shared vision for the college's future.

item.title: Obituaries for September 3
item.description:
Yukie Inaba, 98, of Holualoa died March 26 at Kona Community Hospital. Born on Kauai, she was a junior accountant and member of Daifukuji Soto Mission and Waiaha Kumiai. Private services held; no flowers or koden (monetary gifts). Survived by sons, Brian (Dawn) Inaba and Derek (Renee) Inaba of Kona; daughters, Roxanne (Stan) Sanehira of Hilo and Gail (Matt) Miyasato of Seattle; seven grandchildren and a great-grandson. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

item.title: Funkfit American Samoa claims a First at the 11th Annual Toa Games — in the Scaled Division
item.description:
APIA, SAMOA — Funkfit American Samoa celebrated a historic achievement after claiming first place in the Scaled Division at the 11th Annual Toa Games, a CrossFit-inspired competition hosted by CrossFit Fatu Toa in Apia, Samoa.

Competing against 12 teams, Funkfit delivered a strong and consistent performance throughout the competition to secure a top spot.

The winning team was led by Team Captain Kennedy Nofoagatotoa, alongside teammates Jarret Sunia, Olivia Hogarth, and Alzy Mailei. Together, the four athletes demonstrated strength, endurance, teamwork and determination across the competition’s challenging events.

The victory marks a monumental moment for Funkfit American Samoa, representing the gym’s first Toa Games win in any division.

The team extended special acknowledgement to Coach Claude Young of Funkfit and Walterlee Imo of CrossFit Apia for their leadership, coaching and continued commitment to preparing the athletes leading up to the Toa Games.

Funkfit also thanked their families, friends and the wider community for the tremendous love, encouragement and support they received throughout their journey.

item.title: European Union Naval Force Intercepts Suspected Russian Shadow Fleet Tanker
item.description: Italian Navy multi-purpose combat ship ITS Thaon di Revel (P430), flagship of EU Naval Force Mediterranean Irini, intercepted a Cameroon-flagged oil tanker suspected of being part of Russia’s shadow fleet on Sunday while operating in the Mediterranean. Forces from Thaon di Revel boarded MV Sun (IMO: 9293117) to verify the tanker’s flag. Sun is suspected to be part of Russia’s shadow fleet of merchant vessels and tankers used for sanction evasion. EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas announced the interception in a social media post on Monday. Kallas did not disclose where the boarding took

item.title: After spate of fires Search & Rescue urges residents to take proactive measures
item.description:
Currently investigations have determined these incidents are isolated
By 
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Department of Search and Rescue (DSAR) issued an urgent statement after two major fires last week in the Nuʻuuli area — one at a residential family home and another at a commercial building. 

In their announcement, DSAR- Fire Department highlighted a concerning trend within the community: an increase in fires affecting not only homes but also businesses and surrounding brush areas. While thorough investigations have determined these incidents are isolated and not linked to one another, both the DSAR and its Fire Division take this trend seriously and emphasize the need for community vigilance.

To enhance safety, the DSAR- Fire Department is urging every resident and business owner to take proactive measures. They recommend that individuals closely supervise cooking areas to prevent accidents, stay alert for unusual odors or signs of smoke, and unplug appliances when not in use. Additionally, residents are encouraged to test their smoke alarms monthly and ensure all family members know a clear, unobstructed exit route in an emergency. 

For business owners, recommendations include keeping emergency exits clear and avoiding overloaded electrical circuits, which can pose a fire hazard. Also, remove dry brush and dead leaves from around building perimeters to prevent fires from spreading.

Last Wednesday night, a fire erupted around 10:30 PM in the Lions Park area on Lima Street, becoming the latest incident in a troubling series of approximately two dozen fires reported across American Samoa over the last three months. The fire began within a small, three-building compound situated adjacent to an ASTCA tower and communications building. Eyewitnesses at the park's ball courts, alarmed by the flames, quickly rushed over to assess the situation and determine whether anyone needed assistance.

Witnesses reported that the blaze's intense heat ignited not only a building and a nearby gazebo, but also nearby palm trees. 

In addition to the tireless efforts of first responders, ASTCA employees joined the effort to safeguard nearby communications equipment from potential damage. Workers from Samoa Motors also arrived promptly to help relocate vehicles parked in their lot across the street, ensuring emergency vehicles had unencumbered access.

Then, on Friday morning, tragedy struck again when a house fire broke out in Nuʻuuli, located behind the pool hall next to Alora’s restaurant. The incident sent one person to the hospital, making it the fourth major fire in American Samoa this month.

Neighbors reported that the house was occupied when the fire ignited around 7:30 am. Photographs posted to facebook taken at the scene showed the residence fully engulfed in smoke, with flames licking through cracks in the roof.

One eyewitness recounted the dramatic scene, noting that one person was successfully removed from the burning home and subsequently taken away by ambulance for medical care. Emergency responders extinguished the fire within about two hours, working diligently to prevent further damage. Firefighters later confirmed that the fire was linked to a vehicle parked near the house, underscoring the need for public awareness about fire safety.

This statement and the subsequent incidents underscore the heightened fire risks the community faces and the importance of preventive actions to protect lives and property.

Local News

item.description:
Robert Avery Kalani Bechert, 62, of Hilo died June 28 at Pali Momi Medical Center in Aiea, Oahu. Born on Oahu, he was a state corrections officer. Private celebration of life for family and close friends noon-4 p.m. Oct. 3. Survived by fiancée, Holly Chung of Hilo; mother, Henrietta “Penny” Bechert-Wong of Volcano; daughters, Samantha “Sami” Bechert of Hilo and Savannah “Kahala” Bechert of Mountain View; stepchildren, Gary Napoleon Jr. of Hilo, Kimberly (Dean) Hess of Pahoa and Haily Napoleon of Keaau; sisters, Sherilyn (Jim) Vogt of Alaska, Lisa Lei Lai, Leianne (James) Pedro and Lindsey (Chris) Daniels-Montizor; brother, Peter Daniels of Honolulu; two grandsons and two step-grandsons; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Ballard Family Mortuary.
